Republic of the Philippines DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT DILG-NAPOLCOM center, EDSA corner Quezon Avenue, West Triangle, Quezon City http: //www.dilg.com.ph DILG OPINION No. 71 s. 2023 Mr. PABLO M. CRESPO SR. Secretary of the Mayor Municipality of Patnongon Province of Antique Dear Mr. Crespo: This refers to your letter dated April 18, 2023 requesting this Department's legal opinion on whether or not the Officer-in-Charge, Office of the Mayor can call a special session of the Sangguniang Bayan. Cited in your letter is Section 52 (b) of Republic Act No. 7160, otherwise known as the Local Government Code of 1991 (hereinafter referred to as the Code), which provides that "When public interest so demands, special sessions may be called by the local chief executive or by a majority of the members of the sanggunian." In light of this provision, it is inquired whether or not the OIC, Office of the Mayor can call a special session of the Sangguniang Bayan. In reply thereto, we deemed it necessary to touch upon the signification of the term "officer-in-charge" or OIC, and this is best understood when it is distinguished from the term "acting". Both terms are employed in the context of designation, but they substantially differ in that the latter entails the exercise of both ministerial functions and the exercise of discretion, while the former exercises only ministerial functions— limited. The Civil Service Commission, in its Resolution No. 000778, dated March 24, 2000, expounded thus: "[A] designation under acting capacity may be differentiated from a designation as Officer-in-Charge (OIC) in such a manner that an OIC enjoys limited powers which are confined to functions of administration and ensuring that the office continues its usual activities. The OIC may not be deemed to possess the power to appoint employees as the same involves the exercise of discretion which is beyond the power of an OIC. On the other hand, as aptly ruled by the Commission in the case of Amado S. Day, a designation in an acting capacity entails not only the exercise of the ministerial functions attached to the position but also the exercise of discretion. This is so considering that the person designated is deemed to be the incumbent of the position." As could be clearly gathered from the foregoing, an OIC exercises solely ministerial functions. This now beckons the pivotal question as to what constitutes ministerial functions. CamScanner

In Mallari v. Banco Filipino (G.R. No. 157660, dated August 29, 2009), the Supreme Court had occasion to expound on this term by distinguishing it with the term "discretionary", thus: "A clear line demarcates a discretionary act from a ministerial one. Thus: The distinction between a ministerial and discretionary act is well delineated. A purely ministerial act or duty is one which an officer or tribunal performs in a given state of facts, in a prescribed manner, in obedience to the mandate of a legal authority, without regard to or the exercise of his own judgment upon the propriety or impropriety of the act done. If the law imposes a duty upon a public officer and gives him the right to decide how or when the duty shall be performed, such duty is discretionary and not ministerial. The duty is ministerial only when the discharge of the same requires neither the exercise of official discretion or judgment." Further, the pronouncement of the Supreme Court in the Symaco v. Aquino is instructive, thus: "Ministerial duty is one which is so clear and specific as to leave no room for the exercise of discretion in its performance. On the other hand, a discretionary duty is that which by its nature requires the exercise of judgment. A purely ministerial act or duty is one in which an officer or tribunal performs in a given state of facts, in a prescribed manner, in obedience to the mandate of legal authority, without regard to or the exercise of his own judgment, upon the propriety of the act done. But if the law imposes a duty upon a public officer and gives him the right to decide how or when the duty shall be performed, such duty is discretionary and not ministerial. The duty is ministerial only when the discharge of the same requires neither the exercise of official discretion nor judgment." Premised from the foregoing, it is this level's view that the conduct of special sessions, as provided for under Section 52(b) of the Code, is well within the purview of the functions pertaining to the exercise of discretion; it involves the determination of what may be deemed "public interest"—a discretionary act—and thus may not be performed by an OIC. This opinion is being rendered based solely on the facts as represented and without prejudice to any contrary opinion of competent authorities and the courts. We hope to have guided you accordingly. Thank you. Very truly yours, By thority of the Secreta ATTY. NV OR R. LLAMAS ecretary for External, Legal and Legislative Affairs and co urrent OIC, LLLS OUSELWJVRULLLS-LRALLD0a DIR. JOVIAN E.
